faqs.question: Do you cover Scotland and Wales?
faqs.answer: Yes. Heimdell Tech Ai works with businesses across the whole United Kingdom: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It is based in Preston, Lancashire, and delivers its AI agent readiness, software and TPV compliance services remotely and nationwide.

faqs.question: What is AI agent readiness?
faqs.answer: AI agent readiness means a business can be found, understood and transacted with by software acting for a customer, such as AI assistants and shopping agents. It covers accurate structured data, clear prices and policies, a simple way to book or buy, and support for open standards such as A2A, AP2, UCP and MCP. Heimdell Tech Ai helps UK businesses get there.
aliases: make my business ready for AI agents

faqs.question: Is there a free way to check how AI agents see my website?
faqs.answer: Yes. The free agent-readiness scanner on the Heimdell Tech Ai homepage scores a website out of 100, shows the most important fixes and can email the full report. It only reads publicly available pages.
aliases: check my website for AI agents

faqs.question: What does the agent-readiness scanner check?
faqs.answer: It checks whether AI crawlers are blocked in robots.txt, whether there is a sitemap and an llms.txt file, schema.org structured data, whether product data is complete (price, currency, availability, image, identifier), whether policy pages state concrete terms, whether there is a clear booking or checkout path, and whether the site publishes an A2A Agent Card or a UCP profile.

faqs.question: How much does AI agent readiness cost?
faqs.answer: The scan is free. Implementation work is custom and bespoke: every project is scoped and quoted individually, so there is no fixed published price. A quote can be requested at heimdell-tech-ai.co.uk/contact.html.

faqs.question: Can Heimdell Tech Ai guarantee more customers from AI agents?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody honestly can yet. Heimdell Tech Ai measures how AI assistants describe a business before and after the work and shows the difference.

faqs.question: Which AI agent standards does Heimdell Tech Ai work with?
faqs.answer: A2A (Agent2Agent), AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol), UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol), MCP (Model Context Protocol) and Google Cloud Knowledge Catalog, together with the structured data and policy foundations they all rely on.

faqs.question: What is the difference between A2A, AP2, UCP and MCP?
faqs.answer: A2A lets AI agents talk to each other and hand over tasks. AP2 covers how an agent is authorised to pay on a customer's behalf. UCP covers browsing a catalogue, managing a cart and checking out. MCP connects an AI assistant to tools and data. Knowledge Catalog organises and describes business data so agents can trust it. Most businesses need only one or two of these.

faqs.question: Do I need to support every AI agent standard?
faqs.answer: No. Most businesses should start with accurate structured data, clear prices and policies and a simple way to book or buy. Standards such as A2A, AP2 and UCP are added where they give a real benefit. Several are still changing, so the current specification is checked before anything is built.

faqs.question: Who is AI agent readiness for?
faqs.answer: UK businesses that customers may find through AI assistants: online shops, hotels and restaurants, clinics and local services, and any business whose prices, availability or policies customers ask about.

faqs.question: What is the A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol?
faqs.answer: A2A is an open standard that lets AI agents built by different vendors discover each other, exchange messages and hand over tasks. It was launched by Google in 2025, is hosted by the Linux Foundation, and reached version 1.0 in March 2026. Heimdell Tech Ai implements it for UK businesses, from the Agent Card to booking integration.

faqs.question: What is an A2A Agent Card?
faqs.answer: An Agent Card is a machine-readable description of what a business or agent can do and how to reach it, published on its own domain. Other agents read it to discover capabilities such as checking availability, requesting a quote or booking an appointment. Heimdell Tech Ai publishes its own at heimdell-tech-ai.co.uk/.well-known/agent-card.json.

faqs.question: Does A2A replace my website?
faqs.answer: No. A2A sits alongside your website and booking system and gives AI agents a structured way in.

faqs.question: What is AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol)?
faqs.answer: AP2 is an open protocol, created by Google and donated to the FIDO Alliance in April 2026, that lets an AI agent make a payment on a customer's behalf. It uses signed records of what the customer authorised, so every agent purchase has verifiable proof. Heimdell Tech Ai implements it for UK businesses.
aliases: how do AI agents pay for things
can AI agents pay for things

faqs.question: What is a mandate in AP2?
faqs.answer: A mandate is a signed record of what a customer has authorised an AI agent to do, such as what it may buy and any limits. Mandates give each agent purchase tamper-evident proof of authorisation.
aliases: how does an AI agent get permission to spend

faqs.question: What is a 'human not present' payment in AP2?
faqs.answer: AP2 version 0.2, released in April 2026, added 'human not present' payments, where an agent completes a purchase on pre-authorised instructions without the customer being there, for example buying limited-release tickets the moment they go on sale.

faqs.question: What is the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)?
faqs.answer: UCP is an open standard announced by Google in January 2026 and co-developed with Shopify. It lets AI agents discover a merchant's products, understand what the merchant supports and complete a purchase inside a conversation. Merchants publish a profile, conventionally at /.well-known/ucp. Heimdell Tech Ai checks UCP profiles and the product data behind them.
aliases: how do AI agents buy from my shop

faqs.question: Do I need to do anything for UCP if I use Shopify?
faqs.answer: Shopify stores can publish a UCP profile automatically, so there is often little protocol work to do. The bigger job is usually the quality of product data and the clarity of policies, which is what agents actually read.

faqs.question: Is UCP the same as AP2?
faqs.answer: No. UCP covers commerce: reading a catalogue, managing a cart and checking out. AP2 covers payments: how an agent is authorised to pay on a customer's behalf. They are designed to work together.

faqs.question: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
faqs.answer: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. Anthropic introduced it in late 2024 and donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. Heimdell Tech Ai designs and builds MCP servers that expose chosen tools to assistants with permissions the client controls.

faqs.question: How is MCP different from A2A?
faqs.answer: MCP connects an AI assistant to tools and data, such as a booking system. A2A connects AI agents to each other, so one agent can hand a task to another. They solve different problems and are often used together.

faqs.question: Is it safe to let an AI assistant use my systems through MCP?
faqs.answer: It can be, if the connection is designed carefully. Heimdell Tech Ai exposes only the specific tools the client chooses, keeps them read-only unless told otherwise, requires approval for anything that changes data, and logs every request.

faqs.question: What is Google Cloud Knowledge Catalog?
faqs.answer: Knowledge Catalog is Google Cloud's metadata management platform, formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog. It discovers data assets, organises them, and adds business context such as descriptions, glossaries, data quality and lineage so that people and AI agents can find and trust data. Heimdell Tech Ai helps businesses prepare their data for it and for AI agent use.

faqs.question: Is Knowledge Catalog the same as Dataplex?
faqs.answer: It is the renamed Dataplex Universal Catalog. Google renamed it in April 2026, and the API, command-line and permission names did not change.

faqs.question: Do I need Google Cloud to make my business data agent-ready?
faqs.answer: No. The principle is the same on any platform: accurate, structured, well-described facts about your business that agents can read. Heimdell Tech Ai can build that foundation with or without Google Cloud, including structured data, an llms.txt guide and a curated knowledge base.

faqs.question: What does Heimdell Tech Ai do?
faqs.answer: Heimdell Tech Ai Ltd is a UK software development and IT consultancy in Preston, Lancashire. It helps businesses get ready for AI agents (A2A, AP2, UCP, MCP and Knowledge Catalog), builds custom software, apps, websites and AI systems, and also runs managed third-party verification (TPV) and compliance services for UK telecom sales teams.

faqs.question: Does Heimdell Tech Ai still offer third-party verification (TPV)?
faqs.answer: Yes. Heimdell Tech Ai still runs managed third-party verification for UK telecom resellers, brokers and sales teams, with audit-ready certificates from 80p per phone verification. Details are at heimdell-tech-ai.co.uk/tpv-commission-protection.html and /third-party-verification.html.

faqs.question: What happens if a customer refuses to complete the verification call?
faqs.answer: If a customer refuses or hangs up before verification is complete, the sale is logged as unverified rather than confirmed — it isn't recorded as a pass. In practice this means the agent or provider is alerted immediately so the sale can be followed up, re-attempted, or withdrawn before it's treated as a confirmed order.

faqs.question: What happens if the verification call goes unanswered or to voicemail?
faqs.answer: An unanswered call doesn't count as a completed verification — the system logs it as a failed attempt and the call is retried within the verification window. If the customer still can't be reached, the sale stays unverified until contact is made, protecting you from treating an unconfirmed order as a completed sale.

faqs.question: Does the verification call replace the welcome call some providers require?
faqs.answer: No — a verification call and a welcome call serve different purposes. The verification call independently confirms identity, contract terms, cooling-off rights and Direct Debit authority at the point of sale; a welcome call (where a provider requires one) is typically a later relationship-building touchpoint and isn't a substitute for independently verified consent evidence.

faqs.question: Can verification be done by SMS or link instead of a phone call?
faqs.answer: Yes — link verification is available as a lighter-touch alternative for straightforward cases, costing 1 credit compared to 5 credits for a full phone verification. Phone verification remains the more thorough option since it captures a recorded, agent-led conversation covering identity, terms, cooling-off rights and Direct Debit authority.

faqs.question: How much does a single phone verification cost?
faqs.answer: A phone verification costs 5 credits, which works out to roughly 80p–£1 depending on the credit bundle you buy. Credits are sold on a pay-as-you-go basis — £20 for 100 credits, £90 for 500, or £320 for 2,000 — with no subscription or setup fee.

faqs.question: Is there a subscription, contract or setup fee to use the service?
faqs.answer: No — there's no subscription, no contract and no setup fee. You buy credits as you need them (£20/100, £90/500, £320/2,000) and each phone verification uses 5 credits, so you only pay for verifications you actually run.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a verification call and a standard sales quality-assurance (QA) call?
faqs.answer: A QA call is typically an internal spot-check on a small sample of sales calls to monitor agent performance, while a verification call is an independent check run on every relevant sale to confirm the customer's consent. QA reviews process; verification creates the evidence record that proves the sale itself was valid.

faqs.question: Can my commission still be clawed back even after a sale has passed verification?
faqs.answer: Yes — verification protects you against disputes over consent, but it doesn't prevent every clawback. Commissions can still be reversed for reasons unrelated to consent, such as the customer cancelling within a provider's clawback window or failing to pay, since those are billing and churn outcomes rather than consent disputes.

faqs.question: Is third party verification a legal requirement for UK telecom sales, or just best practice?
faqs.answer: In the UK, third party verification isn't a single named legal mandate the way it is in the US under FCC rules — it's a best-practice mechanism telecom resellers use to demonstrate compliance with Ofcom's General Conditions on consent, contract transparency and mis-selling. Many providers require it contractually even where it isn't a standalone statutory obligation.

faqs.question: Who actually makes the verification call — is it in-house staff or an independent third party?
faqs.answer: The verification call is made by an independent agent who isn't involved in the original sale, not by the salesperson or their own team. That independence is what gives the verification evidentiary weight — a self-recorded confirmation by the seller carries far less credibility with providers and regulators.

faqs.question: Does the customer have to pay for the verification call?
faqs.answer: No — the verification call is free for the customer to receive. The cost is covered by the reseller or provider running the verification, billed in credits (5 credits per phone verification) rather than passed on to the customer.

faqs.question: How does verification interact with the customer's 14-day cooling-off period?
faqs.answer: Verification happens within 24 hours of the sale, well inside the standard 14-day cooling-off period for distance and off-premises telecom contracts. The verification call itself reconfirms the customer's cooling-off rights as part of the conversation, rather than starting or ending the cooling-off clock.

faqs.question: Does the verification platform integrate with our CRM or sales software?
faqs.answer: Yes — verification requests and results sync with your existing sales workflow rather than requiring a separate standalone tool. Each verification's outcome (confirmed, failed or unreachable) is logged and made available to feed back into your CRM or order system.

faqs.question: Is AI-assisted call recording and analysis GDPR and PECR compliant?
faqs.answer: Yes — verification calls are recorded on a clear lawful basis (consent and legitimate business interest for compliance and dispute resolution), with the recording purpose disclosed to the customer on the call. Recordings are stored securely, consistent with UK GDPR and PECR requirements for electronic communications.

faqs.question: How does the system stop a verification recording from being edited or tampered with after the call?
faqs.answer: Each recording is locked and time-stamped at the point of capture, with the resulting compliance certificate tied to that specific, unedited recording. This creates a verifiable record that can't be quietly altered after the fact, which is what gives it weight in a provider audit or dispute.

faqs.question: Does the platform transcribe verification calls automatically?
faqs.answer: Verification calls are recorded in full, and the platform can produce a written record of the call alongside the audio to make reviewing evidence faster during an audit or dispute. The audio recording remains the primary evidence; the transcript is a convenience layer on top of it.

faqs.question: How are verification credits tracked and billed?
faqs.answer: Credits are deducted automatically each time a verification runs — 5 credits for a phone verification, 1 credit for a link verification — with no manual invoicing step. You top up credits as needed (£20/100, £90/500, £320/2,000) and can see usage as verifications are completed.

faqs.question: Does the system check that every required disclosure is actually covered on the call?
faqs.answer: Yes — verification calls follow a structured process covering identity confirmation, contract terms, cooling-off rights and Direct Debit authority, so a call isn't marked as verified unless each of those points is addressed. This guards against incomplete or rushed verifications being logged as valid.

faqs.question: What technical metadata does the platform log alongside the call recording?
faqs.answer: Alongside the audio recording, the platform logs the call timestamp, duration, and the outcome of each disclosure point covered, all attached to the resulting compliance certificate. This metadata is what makes a single verification record searchable and auditable rather than just an audio file.

faqs.question: Does the platform support digital or link-based verification as well as phone calls?
faqs.answer: Yes — alongside full phone verification, the platform supports a lighter-touch link verification option at 1 credit per use, versus 5 credits for a phone call. This gives resellers a faster option for lower-risk verifications while keeping phone verification as the more thorough method.

faqs.question: Is verification data stored securely?
faqs.answer: Yes — call recordings, transcripts and compliance certificates are stored securely rather than kept as loose local files, so they remain accessible and intact when needed for a provider audit or dispute months later.

faqs.question: Can multiple sales agents or office locations use the platform under one account?
faqs.answer: Yes — the platform is built to handle verification requests from multiple agents or sales locations feeding into the same account, with credits shared centrally rather than needing a separate account per agent or office.

faqs.question: What happens in the system when a verification fails or the customer's answers don't match the contract?
faqs.answer: A failed or mismatched verification is logged as such rather than silently discarded, flagging the sale for follow-up instead of letting it pass through as confirmed. That failed-verification record is itself useful evidence — it shows the sale was checked and didn't hold up, rather than never being checked at all.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a provider audit and an Ofcom investigation?
faqs.answer: A provider audit is a commercial review carried out by the network or service provider (like Virgin Media, O2 or Sky) checking a reseller's own sales practices and paperwork, while an Ofcom investigation is a regulatory action under the General Conditions, usually triggered by wider complaint patterns or a formal referral. Passing provider audits consistently reduces the chance of ever reaching Ofcom's attention in the first place.

faqs.question: What percentage of my sales calls will an auditor actually review?
faqs.answer: Auditors typically review a sample of your sales rather than every single one — industry-wide call quality audits commonly sample somewhere in the low single-digit percentage of total volume. Because only a fraction of calls are checked, having consistent, complete verification records across all sales matters more than hoping the ones reviewed happen to be clean.

faqs.question: Can I lose my reseller agreement completely after repeated audit failures?
faqs.answer: Yes — providers can terminate a reseller agreement after a pattern of repeated audit failures, not just after a single incident. A history of failed audits, unresolved findings or rising complaint rates is what typically escalates from a warning to suspension to termination.

faqs.question: Does having verification records guarantee I'll pass a provider audit?
faqs.answer: No — verification records are strong evidence of consent, but auditors also review complaint handling, contract documentation, agent training and clawback history. Verification covers the consent side of the audit thoroughly; it's one major piece of a broader compliance picture, not the whole picture.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a scheduled audit and an unannounced spot check?
faqs.answer: A scheduled audit is planned in advance, giving you time to prepare documentation, while a spot check or mystery shop happens without warning to see how sales actually run day to day. Because spot checks can't be prepped for in the moment, the only real defence is having verification and documentation practices consistently in place, not switched on before a known audit date.

faqs.question: Is a One Touch Switch (OTS) compliance review the same as a standard provider sales audit?
faqs.answer: No — a One Touch Switch review checks your switching process specifically (how gaining and losing provider handoffs are handled), while a standard provider sales audit looks more broadly at consent, contract terms and sales conduct. A reseller can be fully OTS-compliant and still fail a broader sales audit, or vice versa, since they check different things.

faqs.question: What happens to commission I've already been paid if an audit finds a problem with the sale?
faqs.answer: If an audit uncovers a problem with a specific sale — such as unclear consent or a misrepresented term — the commission already paid on that sale is typically clawed back retroactively. This is separate from routine churn-based clawbacks; it's tied directly to the audit finding a fault with how the sale was made.

faqs.question: Why can't I just review my own sales calls instead of using an independent verification service?
faqs.answer: You can review your own calls, but providers and regulators give self-reviewed records far less weight than independently verified ones, since the seller has an obvious interest in the outcome. Independent verification removes that conflict of interest, which is exactly what auditors are looking to confirm is in place.

faqs.question: What documents do auditors ask for beyond the verification recording itself?
faqs.answer: Beyond the verification recording, auditors commonly ask for the signed or accepted contract, complaint logs, agent training records, and a history of clawback or cancellation rates. The verification recording proves consent at the point of sale; these other documents show the wider process around it was sound.

faqs.question: How long does a provider audit take from notification to final outcome?
faqs.answer: Timelines vary by provider, but once notified you should expect a review period of several weeks covering document submission, sample review and any follow-up queries before a final outcome is issued. This is distinct from how far ahead you should prepare — ongoing readiness matters more than the length of the audit itself once it starts.

faqs.question: What is GC C1 under Ofcom's General Conditions, and how does it affect my commission?
faqs.answer: GC C1 is the Ofcom General Condition requiring telecom providers to give customers clear, accurate and up-to-date information on pricing, contract terms and exit charges before they sign up. Gaps here — an incomplete verbal price disclosure, a missing contract summary, no timestamped consent record — are the exact evidence providers point to when reversing a sale and clawing back the commission on it. A GC C1 audit checks whether your sales process actually meets the standard before it becomes a dispute.

faqs.question: What is 'slamming' and why does it lead to commission clawbacks?
faqs.answer: Slamming is Ofcom's term for switching a customer's telecom service without their knowledge or genuine consent, and it's one of the clearest triggers for both regulatory action and commission reversal. Ofcom has fined and named providers over slamming cases involving elderly or vulnerable customers, and any sale later found to be a slam is almost always unwound, with commission clawed back from the agent or agency that closed it.

faqs.question: Does the 14-day cooling-off period mean my commission isn't safe until it expires?
faqs.answer: Cancellations made within the 14-day statutory cooling-off period are a common commission clawback trigger, since the sale can be unwound penalty-free under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013. This right generally doesn't apply to in-person, doorstep-style sales, which is why D2D teams face a different clawback risk profile than telesales teams selling by phone.

faqs.question: What is One Touch Switch, and does it add new commission clawback risk?
faqs.answer: One Touch Switch (OTS) is Ofcom's process, introduced under General Conditions C7.18-C7.27, that makes the customer's new provider responsible for organising a broadband or landline switch. Because OTS shifts more of the switching process — and the paper trail — onto the acquiring provider, gaps in how a sale is logged at the point of switch are now more visible and more likely to surface later as a clawback dispute.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a non-pay clawback and a mis-sell clawback?
faqs.answer: A non-pay clawback happens when a customer never completes payment or defaults early, while a mis-sell clawback happens when the sale itself is found non-compliant — no valid consent, incomplete disclosure, or a slammed switch. Non-pay clawbacks are largely about customer creditworthiness; mis-sell clawbacks are about your sales process, which is what a compliance audit is built to fix.

faqs.question: Can a provider claw back commission months after the sale has already closed?
faqs.answer: Yes — clawback windows commonly extend to a customer's first 30, 60 or 90 days, and some provider agreements allow clawback for the length of an early-cancellation clause, not just the initial cooling-off period. The longer the window, the more it matters that your consent and disclosure records are still retrievable and audit-ready when a dispute is raised.

faqs.question: How do I dispute or challenge a commission clawback?
faqs.answer: The strongest defence against a clawback is documentary evidence that the sale was compliant at the point of sale — recorded consent, a contract summary provided, correct pricing disclosed. Without a timestamped audit trail, most disputes come down to the provider's word against the agent's, which is why unclear or open-ended clawback clauses are flagged as a risk area for the paying company too, not just the seller.

faqs.question: What percentage of gross commission do UK telecom agencies typically lose to clawbacks?
faqs.answer: UK telecom agencies typically lose 5-15% of gross commissions annually to clawbacks, disputes and reversals. That range is wide because it depends heavily on how consistently a sales team captures and retains compliant point-of-sale evidence, which is exactly what a clawback audit is designed to tighten up.

faqs.question: What does a free 15-minute commission clawback audit actually check?
faqs.answer: It's a short review of your current sales verification process against GC C1 and related Ofcom General Conditions, looking for the specific gaps — missing consent records, incomplete disclosures, weak vulnerable-customer safeguards — that providers use as grounds to claw back commission. It's designed to quantify how much revenue you're likely leaking to clawbacks, not to replace a full compliance implementation.

faqs.question: How much can Ofcom fine a telecom provider for breaching the General Conditions, and why does that matter to my commission?
faqs.answer: Ofcom can fine providers up to 10% of turnover for General Conditions breaches, and it has issued penalties as high as £28 million for systemic failures such as blocking customer cancellations. When a provider is under that kind of regulatory pressure, it tightens its own compliance checks on agency-sold contracts, and clawback activity on non-compliant sales tends to rise as a result.

faqs.question: What is PECR and how does it apply to telecom sales calls?
faqs.answer: PECR (the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations 2003) is separate UK law that sits alongside UK GDPR and specifically governs marketing calls, texts, emails and cookies. For telecom sales teams it sets the rules on which numbers you can call, what consent you need, and what you must disclose during the call — breaching it carries its own ICO fines regardless of your GDPR compliance status.

faqs.question: What are the legal hours for telemarketing calls under PECR?
faqs.answer: Unsolicited marketing calls are only permitted between 8am and 8pm on weekdays and 9am and 6pm on weekends and public holidays. Calling outside these windows, or calling a number registered with the Telephone Preference Service without prior consent, is a PECR breach the ICO actively enforces against.

faqs.question: What is the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) and do I have to screen against it before calling?
faqs.answer: The TPS is the UK's official opt-out register for unsolicited sales and marketing calls, and PECR requires specific consent to call a TPS-registered number for marketing purposes. Skipping TPS screening is one of the most common breaches cited in real ICO enforcement notices against telemarketing firms.

faqs.question: What is the 'soft opt-in' and can telecom resellers use it to contact existing customers?
faqs.answer: The soft opt-in lets you market similar products to existing customers without separate explicit consent, but only if their details were collected during an actual sale, they were given a clear opt-out at the time, and every message since has included one. It does not apply to prospects or bought-in contact lists — those still need explicit consent under PECR.

faqs.question: What is DUAA 2025 and when does it take effect?
faqs.answer: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 is the UK's reform of data protection law. It received royal assent on 19 June 2025 and is rolling out in phases, with most provisions taking effect from 5 February 2026 and final measures following in June 2026. It amends UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and PECR rather than replacing them outright.

faqs.question: Does DUAA 2025 replace UK GDPR?
faqs.answer: No — DUAA amends UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and PECR with targeted changes rather than replacing them. The six lawful bases for processing, core data subject rights and the accountability principle all remain in place, so an existing UK GDPR compliance programme needs updating for DUAA, not rebuilding from scratch.

faqs.question: What is 'Recognised Legitimate Interest' under DUAA 2025?
faqs.answer: It's a new, seventh lawful basis for processing personal data that DUAA adds to UK GDPR, covering specific purposes such as safeguarding vulnerable people, preventing crime or assisting public bodies, without the usual legitimate-interests balancing test. It's narrower than general legitimate interest and doesn't extend to ordinary telecom sales and marketing activity.

faqs.question: How much can the ICO actually fine a business for a PECR or UK GDPR breach?
faqs.answer: For the most serious UK GDPR breaches the ICO can fine up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher; a lower tier of up to £8.7 million or 2% applies to less severe breaches. PECR marketing breaches are enforced separately and have resulted in fines up to £500,000 against telemarketing firms.

faqs.question: What fines have real telemarketing companies received from the ICO recently?
faqs.answer: Recent ICO enforcement includes a £90,000 fine against a compensation firm for unlawful marketing calls, £340,000 split across two companies for aggressive and unwanted calls, and a historic £500,000 fine against CRDNN for over 193 million automated nuisance calls. The ICO has issued more than £2.4 million in PECR fines since April 2022 alone.

faqs.question: Do the DUAA 2025 changes affect PECR marketing rules for telecom sales teams?
faqs.answer: Yes — DUAA makes targeted amendments to PECR alongside UK GDPR, and ICO enforcement powers under both are being strengthened as part of the same Act, including the ability to compel witnesses and demand reports during investigations. A regulatory risk assessment needs to check PECR marketing practices against both the current rules and the DUAA changes taking effect through 2026.

faqs.question: What is the deadline for responding to a Subject Access Request (SAR)?
faqs.answer: You must respond to a SAR without undue delay and within one calendar month of receipt, extendable by a further two months for complex or numerous requests. The clock starts the day the request arrives — including non-working days — and can only be paused if you need to request clarification from the requester.

faqs.question: What happens if my business misses the SAR deadline?
faqs.answer: A missed SAR deadline is a UK GDPR compliance failure the ICO can investigate, and it weakens your position if the requester complains directly to the regulator. Most SAR failures stem from not having a clear process for locating, verifying and redacting data quickly enough — exactly what SAR-response readiness testing in a compliance audit is meant to catch before a real request arrives.

faqs.question: Does DUAA 2025 change how businesses must handle Subject Access Requests?
faqs.answer: Yes — under DUAA, businesses are only required to carry out 'reasonable and proportionate' searches when responding to a SAR, rather than an exhaustive search of every system. This gives some relief on scope, but the one-month response deadline itself is unchanged, so SAR processes still need to be fast and well-documented.

faqs.question: What counts as a data breach that has to be reported to the ICO within 72 hours?
faqs.answer: Only breaches likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms must be reported to the ICO, and the 72-hour clock starts the moment you become aware of the breach, not when it happened. A breach assessed as unlikely to cause harm doesn't need ICO notification, but it must still be logged internally — a distinction many businesses get wrong.

faqs.question: What's the penalty for failing to report a data breach within 72 hours?
faqs.answer: Failing to notify the ICO of a reportable breach carries its own fine of up to £8.7 million or 2% of global annual turnover, separate from any fine for the breach itself. The 72 hours are clock hours, not working hours, so there's no pause for weekends or bank holidays.

faqs.question: What is a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and when is one required?
faqs.answer: A DPIA is a structured risk assessment of a data processing activity, required under UK GDPR whenever processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals — such as large-scale customer data processing or systematic monitoring. It must be completed before the processing activity begins, examining data flows, legal basis and security controls.

faqs.question: Is an ICO audit something that happens to you, or can you request one voluntarily?
faqs.answer: ICO audits can be either consensual — requested or agreed voluntarily — or compulsory, where the ICO uses its Data Protection Act 2018 powers to assess an organisation's practices. A voluntary, ICO-aligned self-audit in advance lets a business fix gaps on its own terms rather than under investigation.

faqs.question: What's the difference between UK GDPR and PECR, and does a GDPR audit cover both?
faqs.answer: UK GDPR governs how personal data is processed generally, while PECR is a separate set of regulations specifically covering marketing calls, texts, emails and cookies — a telecom sales team can be fully UK GDPR compliant and still breach PECR through its calling practices. A proper compliance audit needs to check both, since the ICO enforces them independently with separate fines for each.

faqs.question: Can I refuse or redact part of a Subject Access Request?
faqs.answer: Yes — SAR responses can exclude third-party personal data unless that person consents or it's reasonable to disclose without consent, and statutory exemptions such as legal privilege or crime prevention can also apply. Identity verification is a legitimate reason to pause the process, but it must be proportionate rather than used to stall a genuine request.
